name: H.C. Erik Midelfort
specialization: Southwestern German witchcraft prosecutions; cascade and panic dynamics; gender analysis of accused

major_works.title: Witch Hunting in Southwestern Germany 1562-1684
major_works.significance: First major regional German witchcraft study; developed the cascade model of prosecution panics; challenged simple misogyny thesis through gender data

major_works.title: A History of Madness in Sixteenth-Century Germany
major_works.significance: Extends analysis of social-psychological dynamics to madness and possession in same period

core_argument: Large-scale witch panics in southwestern Germany followed a cascade logic: initial prosecutions led to confessions naming accomplices, which expanded the accused pool, until the accused began to include people of high social status, at which point prosecutions collapsed. Gender analysis reveals that while women predominated in small-scale prosecutions, large panics ensnared substantial numbers of men, complicating simple misogyny explanations.

methodological_approach.primary_materials: Trial records from over 1,200 prosecutions in southwestern German territories (Breisgau, Württemberg, Alsace, episcopal territories) 1562-1684
methodological_approach.analysis_target: Gender and social status of accused; prosecution scale and duration; timing of panic onset and collapse
methodological_approach.evidence_type: Quantitative statistical analysis of regional prosecution records; comparative case studies of small vs. large panics
methodological_approach.explanatory_level: Regional structural: legal institutions and social dynamics interacting to produce varying prosecution intensities

key_contributions.claim: Witch panics expanded through forced denunciation: each accused named accomplices under torture, creating chains of accusation that could encompass hundreds
key_contributions.implication: The scale of large persecutions was a procedural artifact as much as a reflection of underlying belief

key_contributions.claim: While women made up the majority of accused in small-scale prosecutions, large panics showed substantially higher male representation, sometimes approaching parity
key_contributions.implication: Simple misogyny explanations for witch-hunting require qualification; gender dynamics varied by prosecution scale

key_contributions.concept: Social status threshold for panic collapse
key_contributions.claim: Prosecutions tended to collapse when accusation chains reached persons of high social standing whose guilt was socially implausible
key_contributions.implication: Social structure provided a natural brake on cascading prosecutions

reception_and_critique.major_influences: German legal history, comparative European regional studies, quantitative social history
criticisms: Southwestern Germany may not represent German prosecutions generally
Feminist historians argue the gender complexity finding should not obscure the overall predominance of female victims
Cascade model is descriptive rather than fully explanatory of why some regions panicked and others did not

historiographical_significance: Midelfort's study established the regional monograph as the dominant format for witchcraft scholarship and provided the first rigorous statistical analysis of German prosecutions. His cascade model became a standard analytical tool for understanding large panics. His gender findings generated productive controversy that pushed feminist historiography to greater nuance.
source_method: Published scholarship and critical historiographical reconstruction
